description: ARIRANHA is a group formed by six Information Technology students, united by their shared interest in technology, science, innovation, and creativity.
summary:
ASTRA: Mission Zero is a browser-based game in which players design, manage and simulate a complete space mission. In the hangar, they choose an astronaut, one of three spacecraft (Explorer, Voyager or Titan), and scientific instruments, while respecting a $100 million budget, a cargo mass limit and mandatory launch, fuel and communication costs. The mission then unfolds inside an explorable spacecraft, where players manage fuel, energy and hull integrity. They face space debris, a Martian dust storm, Jupiter’s radiation and a system overheating. They also choose the order of destinations, which changes fuel use and mission duration, and select the right instrument for each scientific discovery. A telemetry chart and final report show how every decision shaped the outcome, from perfect mission to failure, and a mystery about a missing satellite rewards exploration.

The game turns abstract trade-offs, such as cost versus mass, power versus protection, and science versus fuel, into hands-on decisions with visible consequences. This matters because students rarely experience a mission from concept to operation. Planet information follows NASA sources, a Women in Space section honors real pioneers, and costs and resource values are fictional gameplay parameters.
details:
ASTRA: Mission Zero is a single-page browser game in which players plan and run an entire space mission, from the first design choices to the final report. The player begins by choosing an astronaut. Then, on a tablet in the hangar, they select one of three spacecraft (Explorer, Voyager or Titan) and a set of scientific instruments. Every choice must fit within a $100 million budget and the ship’s cargo limit, and the player must also cover the mandatory costs of launch, fuel reserve, trajectory planning and monitoring. After launch, the player moves through an explorable spacecraft with five stations: Navigation, Communications, Engineering, Science Lab and Mission Control. Fuel, energy and hull integrity are tracked live and change with every decision. The player chooses the order in which to visit Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, which changes fuel use and mission duration. Each planet brings a hazard, such as a dust storm, intense radiation or a trajectory adjustment, along with a scientific challenge in which the right instrument must be chosen. Along the way, a fictional mystery about a missing satellite rewards exploration, and the clues the player finds decide whether the ending is a full discovery, a partial discovery or a lost signal.

The game turns trade-offs that usually stay abstract, such as cost versus mass, energy versus protection and science versus fuel, into hands-on decisions with visible consequences. Players learn by experimenting, and a telemetry chart and a final report show how each choice shaped the result. The project needs no installation or special hardware, since it runs from a single HTML file in an ordinary laptop browser, with keyboard, mouse and on-screen button controls. Its intended impact is to help students experience a mission from concept to operation, which they rarely get to do, and to build curiosity about planetary science. It also shows that space exploration depends on many people: a Women in Space section presents real pioneers, including a tribute to a Brazilian astrophysicist, to inspire students who may not yet see themselves in science and engineering.

The game was built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, without any external game engine. The HTML Canvas draws the pixel-art planets and characters, the radar and the pseudo-3D spacecraft interior, SVG draws the telemetry chart and the blueprint, and the Web Audio API provides sound alerts. The browser’s localStorage saves the mission, Google Fonts provides the typography, and the Claude AI assistant helped write and refine the code. The game runs on any PC or laptop with a modern browser.

The project is creative because it joins a serious engineering challenge with an investigative story and a cinematic identity of its own. The home screen uses a pixel-art background image, and the interface uses a plum-and-pearl color palette. The command center is a walkable spacecraft rather than a menu, and small activities such as radar scanning, system repair and instrument selection replace plain multiple-choice questions.

The team considered several factors along the way. Planet information and distances follow NASA sources, and the debris event takes place near Earth because that is where most orbital debris is found. Prices and resource points are clearly labeled as fictional gameplay values. Every choice has a cost, so no single strategy wins automatically. The scoring rules were reviewed so that penalties, bonuses and the progress percentage reflect what the player actually did. The game is entirely in US English, works on ordinary computers, offers keyboard and click alternatives, and prevents the player from exceeding the budget or cargo limit or getting stuck inside the spacecraft.
